meta.title: Iraqi elections
sources: Wikipedia: Iraqi parliamentary election articles 1946–2025, the presidential referendums of 1995 and 2002, and the indirect presidential elections 2014–2026 (results, infoboxes and leads)

presEras.label: Saddam's referendums
presEras.blurb: Twice, Saddam Hussein put himself to a 'vote': a yes-or-no referendum with no other candidate, no secrecy worth the name and ration cards hanging over every household. The official results — 99.96 per cent, then a perfect 100 — are recorded here as artefacts of state terror, not elections.

presEras.label: Elected by parliament
presEras.blurb: Under the post-2003 constitution the Council of Representatives elects the president, by convention a Kurd, with a two-thirds majority required on the first ballot. The office is largely ceremonial, but the vote is real — and repeatedly deadlocked, taking a year in 2022 and five months in 2026.

legEras.label: The Hashemite monarchy
legEras.blurb: Parliamentary elections under the British-installed monarchy were managed affairs: a narrow franchise, two-stage voting for most of the era, palace-picked prime ministers and chambers stuffed with notables. The September 1954 election returned almost every deputy unopposed; the 1958 chamber never finished its term — the July revolution shot the king and buried the parliament with him.

legEras.label: Ba'athist rituals
legEras.blurb: Saddam Hussein revived the National Assembly in 1980 as decoration. Every candidate was vetted by the regime, the Ba'ath-led National Progressive Front could not lose, and the chamber had no power worth contesting. These votes are recorded here as rituals of the dictatorship, not elections.

legEras.label: The federal republic
legEras.blurb: The purple-finger election of January 2005 was the first real vote in half a century, held under insurgent fire. Since then Iraq has kept an unbroken run of competitive parliamentary elections — through civil war, the ISIS catastrophe and the Tishreen uprising — even as turnout sagged and governments took months to form.

presidential.summary: A presidential referendum was held in Iraq on October 15, 1995. It was the first direct presidential election in Ba'athist Iraq under the rule of Saddam Hussein, who had seized power through the Revolutionary Command Council (RCC) in 1979.
presidential.caveat: A yes-or-no referendum on Saddam Hussein with no other candidate, open intimidation and no meaningful secrecy. The official figures are recorded here as artefacts of the dictatorship, not as results.

presidential.summary: A presidential referendum took place in Iraq on October 16, 2002. It was the second presidential election under the rule of Saddam Hussein (the first having taken place in 1995).
presidential.caveat: A yes-or-no referendum on Saddam Hussein with no other candidate, open intimidation and no meaningful secrecy. The official figures are recorded here as artefacts of the dictatorship, not as results.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Iraq on 24 July 2014 to elect the President of Iraq for a four-year term via indirect suffrage by the Council of Representatives. The result was a win for Fuad Masum, who received 211 votes.
presidential.caveat: An indirect vote of the Council of Representatives; the presidency is largely ceremonial and by convention held by a Kurd.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Iraq on 2 October 2018 to elect the President of Iraq for a four-year term via indirect suffrage by the Council of Representatives. The result was a win for Barham Salih, who received 219 votes.
presidential.caveat: An indirect vote of the Council of Representatives; the presidency is largely ceremonial and by convention held by a Kurd.

presidential.summary: The Iraqi presidential election of 2022 was held on 13 October 2022 to elect by indirect suffrage the president of Iraq for a four-year term. The position is largely ceremonial, with Iraq being a parliamentary system.
presidential.caveat: An indirect vote of the Council of Representatives, held a year late after repeated failures to reach the two-thirds quorum.

presidential.summary: An indirect election was held for the president of Iraq on 11 April 2026 by the Council of Representatives. Nizar Amidi of the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan was elected in the second round of voting with 227 votes, defeating Muthanna Amin of the Kurdistan Islamic Union with 15 votes.
presidential.caveat: An indirect vote of the Council of Representatives, delayed five months by coalition deadlock; the KDP refused to recognise the result.

legislative.summary: During the al-Suwaidi government (February–June 1946), the electoral law of 1924 was revised. The number of seats in the Chamber of Deputies was increased to 138 and provinces were divided into smaller electoral districts.
legislative.caveat: A managed election of the Hashemite monarchy: narrow franchise, heavy palace influence over candidacies and results, and a parliament that answered to the court more than the voters. Recorded here as history, not a fully free election.

legislative.label: June 1954
legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Iraq on 9 June 1954, although they were delayed until 14 June in some areas due to social upheaval. The Constitutional Union Party remained the largest party in the Chamber of Deputies, winning 50 of the 135 seats, although 53 were won by independents.
legislative.caveat: A managed election of the Hashemite monarchy: narrow franchise, heavy palace influence over candidacies and results, and a parliament that answered to the court more than the voters. Recorded here as history, not a fully free election.

legislative.label: September 1954
legislative.summary: Early parliamentary elections were held in Iraq on 12 September 1954, after the Chamber of Deputies elected in June was dissolved by the King on 3 August. The Constitutional Union Party remained the largest party, winning 94 of the 135 seats, although only 25 seats were actually contested.
legislative.caveat: The most rigged vote of the monarchy: Nuri al-Said dissolved the freshly elected June chamber, suppressed the opposition, and had nearly every seat returned unopposed.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Iraq on 5 May 1958 to elect the members of the Chamber of Deputies. It was the last election in monarchical Iraq.
legislative.caveat: A managed election of the Hashemite monarchy: narrow franchise, heavy palace influence over candidacies and results, and a parliament that answered to the court more than the voters. Recorded here as history, not a fully free election.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Iraq on 24 March 1996. The elections were contested by 689 candidates, although 30 MPs were appointed to represent Iraqi Kurdistan.
legislative.caveat: A ritual of Ba'athist rule: every candidate was vetted by the regime and the National Assembly held no real power. Recorded here as history, not an election.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Iraq on 27 March 2000. The elections were contested by 522 candidates, including 25 women.
legislative.caveat: A ritual of Ba'athist rule: every candidate was vetted by the regime and the National Assembly held no real power. Recorded here as history, not an election.

legislative.label: January 2005
legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Iraq on 30 January 2005 to elect the new National Assembly, alongside governorate elections and a parliamentary election in Kurdistan Region. The 275-member legislature had been created under the Transitional Law during the international occupation.
legislative.caveat: Held under insurgent fire with much of the Sunni Arab electorate boycotting or unable to vote — a landmark, but a wounded one.

legislative.label: December 2005
legislative.summary: The elections took place under a list system, whereby voters chose from a list of parties and coalitions. 230 seats were apportioned among Iraq's 18 governorates based on the number of registered voters in each as of the January 2005 elections, including 59 seats for Baghdad Governorate.
Parliamentary elections were held in Iraq on 7 March 2010. The elections decided the 325 members of the Council of Representatives who would elect the prime minister and president.

The open list form of party-list proportional representation, using the governorates as the constituencies, is the electoral system used. The counting system has been changed slightly from the largest remainder method to the modified Sainte-Laguë method due to a ruling by the Supreme Court of Iraq that the previous method discriminated against smaller parties.
legislative.caveat: Held as ISIS overran Anbar; voting was impossible in parts of the province, and the state lost Mosul weeks after the polls closed.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Iraq on 12 May 2018. The elections decided the 329 members of the Council of Representatives, the country's unicameral legislature, who in turn will elect the Iraqi president and prime minister.

Parliamentary elections were held in Iraq on 10 October 2021. The elections determined the 329 members of the Council of Representatives who in turn elected the Iraqi president and confirmed the prime minister.

The 2021 Iraqi parliamentary election resulted in violent protests in Baghdad as well as a political crisis of eleven months. On 3 August 2022, Muqtada al-Sadr called for snap elections, but was unsuccessful.
